questions.q: According to the three-pass approach, what should the first pass through a paper accomplish?
options: A full line-by-line understanding of the method
A quick decision about whether the paper is worth a deeper read
Reproducing the paper's main result
Memorizing the full reference list
questions.explain: The skimming pass (title, abstract, headings, conclusion, figures) exists to cheaply decide whether a paper deserves more of your time, not to build full understanding.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend reading figures and tables before the surrounding body text?
options: Figures are always placed at the start of a section
Figures usually compress the paper's real contribution into a form you can evaluate in seconds
Body text is typically wrong and figures are more reliable
Journals require figures to be read first
questions.explain: A strong figure often communicates the core result faster than a paragraph of prose, which is why it's read before the surrounding text during the skim.

questions.q: In the deep pass, why read the limitations section before the full results?
options: Limitations sections are usually longer and take more time
To avoid anchoring on the headline number before seeing the caveats
Because limitations always appear before results in every paper
Reviewers require it
questions.explain: Reading limitations first keeps you from fixating on an impressive headline number and only noticing the caveats later, if at all.

questions.q: Why does released code often matter more than the paper's prose for understanding what was actually done?
options: Code is always better documented than the paper
Config files and scripts frequently contain exact hyperparameters and preprocessing steps that never made it into the text
Code is peer reviewed more rigorously than the paper
Papers are not allowed to describe implementation details
questions.explain: Implementation specifics like exact hyperparameters or data preprocessing often only surface in the released code, not in the paper's written description.

questions.q: What is the 'claim-evidence gap' described in this lesson?
options: The time between a paper's submission and its publication
The difference between how strongly a sentence is worded and how strongly the actual data supports it
The number of citations a paper receives after publication
The gap between a paper's abstract and its title
questions.explain: Checking the claim-evidence gap means matching the strength of a sentence like 'significantly outperforms' against the actual numbers, variance, and breadth of evidence behind it.
